```text
    # Find the bottleneck before running

    $ desflow explain shop.yaml

    # List the examples, then download one

    $ desflow examples list

    $ desflow examples get local
```

The shop on this page is the model of the `experiment` example: two packers, an order every 2.5 seconds on average, and 4 seconds of packing on average. Every command runs in one folder and needs no Docker service. `desflow fit` needs the `fit` extra: `uv tool install "desflow[fit]"`, or `pip install "desflow[fit]"`.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Get an Example

`desflow --version` prints the release you installed. `desflow examples list`, or `desflow examples` alone, lists every example with the service it needs, such as `(no service)` or `(odctl up kafka-lite)`:

```bash
desflow --version
desflow examples list
desflow examples
```

`desflow examples get` downloads one example at the release you installed, into a folder named after it:

```bash
desflow examples get experiment --api yaml
```

```text
wrote experiment/yaml/experiment.yaml
wrote experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml
wrote experiment/observed_waits.csv

Find the bottleneck, with no run: cd experiment/yaml && desflow explain experiment_shop.yaml
Run the yaml version: cd experiment/yaml && desflow experiment experiment.yaml
```

The model is `experiment_shop.yaml`, and `experiment.yaml` is the experiment that compares two designs of it. `observed_waits.csv` holds the mean wait measured in the real shop. The line before the last runs `desflow explain` on the model, and the last line is the command that runs the example from its own folder. `--api builder` or `--api low-level` downloads the same example in Python.

`--dest` downloads into another folder, and `--ref` downloads from another tag or branch, such as `main` for an example added after your release:

```bash
desflow examples get experiment --api builder --dest shop --ref main
```

```text
wrote shop/experiment/builder/experiment_example.py
wrote shop/experiment/observed_waits.csv

Run the builder version: cd shop/experiment/builder && python experiment_example.py
```

The builder version goes under `shop/experiment/builder`, and the last line runs it from there. A file that is already there stops the download before anything is written, and `--force` replaces it instead. This line downloads the YAML version again, over the files of the first download, and prints the same lines as the first download:

```bash
desflow examples get experiment --api yaml --force
```

### Check a File Before You Run It

`desflow check` builds each blueprint or builder file you give it, and does not run it. It reports what `desflow run` reports before the clock starts: YAML errors, unknown keys, missing names, unset variables, `!python` references that cannot be imported, and connectors whose extra is missing or whose settings are refused. It does not call `run.before`, contact a broker, a database or a catalog, or run a `!python` function. Importing a `!python` module runs its top-level code, as `desflow run` does. It prints `ok FILE (sim_id ID)` for each valid file and every error of an invalid one, and exits 1 if any file is invalid.

The commands below use a small shop in a file of its own. Its packers come from the variable `PACKERS`, 2 when it is not set, and it holds one test. Save it as `shop.yaml`:

```yaml
# A small shop for the commands of the Command Line page that need a file with a
# variable and a test. The packers come from PACKERS, 2 when it is not set.
# Run it with: desflow run shop.yaml --sample 5
simulation: {sim_id: Shop, factor: 0, random_seed: 42}

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: "${PACKERS:-2}", max_cap: 5}

services:
  packing: {dist: gamma, shape: 4, scale: 1 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.4, spawn: pack}

tasks:
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

stats: basic

run: {until: 10 min}

# desflow test runs the model once at the seed and compares these statistics
tests:
  - name: two packers
    expect:
      tasks.pack.finished: 254
      tasks.pack.wait_mean: {value: 4.592, within: 0.001}
```

A builder file has no `${PACKERS}` variable and no `test` section: its values are Python. `desflow check` and `desflow run` take a builder file too, and [Test a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/analysis/test-a-model/index.md) shows how to test one with pytest.

A low-level script is not a file the command reads. Run it with `python`, and test it with pytest as [Test a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/analysis/test-a-model/index.md) shows.

`desflow check` takes more than one file, and `--var NAME=VALUE` fills `${NAME}` in the files and in the files they include, before the environment does. Repeat `--var` for more variables:

```bash
desflow check shop.yaml
desflow check shop.yaml experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --var PACKERS=3
```

It also warns about a run with no end: an arrival with a `dist` or a `gap` and no `max_events`, in a file with no `run.until`, `run.stop` or `run.segments`. The experiment's shop gives no `until`, because the experiment file gives it, so `check` warns about it and still prints `ok`. A `tests` entry with no seed, in a file with no seed of its own, is reported as `desflow test` reports it.

desflow ships no pre-commit hook. A repository that keeps its blueprints in a folder can add its own to `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. pre-commit passes the changed files as the arguments, which `check` takes:

```text
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: desflow-check
        name: desflow check
        entry: desflow check
        language: system
        files: ^models/.*\.ya?ml$
```

`desflow test` runs the tests that a file holds under `tests`. A test names a seed, an end time and the statistics its run must give. It runs the model once, unpaced, with no ingress and no egress, so a test contacts no service. It prints `ok` for each passing test and each difference of a failing one, and exits 1 if any test fails. A file with no tests prints `no tests`. A builder file reads its tests from a `tests.yaml` in its folder. `--fix` writes the measured statistics into the values that differ, and into a test with none, in place of reporting the differences. Read the changes before you keep them, because a test states its numbers at one seed of one desflow version. [Test a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/analysis/test-a-model/#write-tests-in-the-blueprint) writes tests step by step.

```bash
desflow test shop.yaml
desflow test shop.yaml --fix --var PACKERS=2
```

### Check It Before a Long Run

`desflow explain` reads the model without running it. It draws the model as a graph and works out each resource's [utilisation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#utilisation), the share of its units that the arrivals keep busy. SOURCE is a blueprint, a builder Python file with a module-level `SimulationContext`, or a URI such as `s3://bucket/sims/shop.yaml`. A URI that ends in a folder is refused with its name, such as `Error: no file s3://bucket/models/`.

```bash
desflow explain experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml
```

The same output as text:

```text
Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 0.4/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack (task, rate 0.4/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> exit
Resources
+---------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |    μ | c |   ρ | Wq | L | status |
|----------+-----+------+---+-----+----+---+--------|
| packers  | 0.4 | 0.25 | 2 | 0.8 |  - | - | OK     |
+---------------------------------------------------+
packers by units
+-----------------------+
| c |      ρ | status   |
|---+--------+----------|
| 1 |    1.6 | UNSTABLE |
| 2 |    0.8 | OK       |
| 3 | 0.5333 | OK       |
| 4 |    0.4 | OK       |
+-----------------------+
Bottleneck: packers
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times; run --verify to measure it
Hints for utilisation 0.85:
  packers with 2 units: utilisation 0.8, at most 0.85
  packers with 2 units: utilisation 0.85 at a request every 2.35 seconds (25.5 a minute, 0.425 a second)
```

The packers are at utilisation 0.8: they are busy 80% of the time. An order arrives every 2.5 seconds on average (24 a minute, `rate 0.4/s` in the graph). Each order needs 4 seconds of a packer, and 2 packers share the work. The resources table names its columns with the usual queueing symbols:

- λ (lambda) is the arrival rate, 0.4 orders a second.
- μ (mu) is the rate one packer serves, 0.25 orders a second (4 seconds each).
- ρ (rho) is the utilisation.
- Wq is the mean wait in the queue, and L the mean number of orders in the shop. Both show `-` when no formula applies.

The line `Bottleneck: packers` names the resource with the highest utilisation. Relieving it makes the next busiest resource the bottleneck. The status is `OK` below 0.85, `CONGESTED` from 0.85 and `UNSTABLE` from 1, where the queue grows for as long as the run lasts. The table by units shows that one packer would be `UNSTABLE`. The hints give the units and the arrival rate that reach the target of 0.85. A hint of more units than the resource's `max_cap` also says to raise `max_cap`, because a `current_cap` above `max_cap` is lowered to it.

To keep a resource stable, lower its utilisation or its variability: more units (a higher `current_cap`), a shorter service time, a lower arrival `rate`, or less variable gaps or service times. To test how a consumer of the records copes, do the opposite on purpose. From utilisation 0.85 a resource is congested, with long waits that come and go. Above 1 it is overloaded and its queue grows for as long as the overload lasts.

`--target` sets the utilisation the hints aim for, 0.85 by default. At 1 or above the hints are for deliberate overload. This command uses the shop of [Queues and Capacity](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/index.md), saved as `queues_and_capacity.yaml`:

```bash
desflow explain queues_and_capacity.yaml --target 1.2
```

The end of the output is the hints:

```text
Hints for utilisation 1.2:
  packers with 2 units: utilisation 1.35, at least 1.2, for deliberate overload
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 1.2 at a request every 1.25 seconds (48 a minute, 0.8 a second)
```

With 2 packers the shop runs at utilisation 1.35, above the target of 1.2. With 1 packer, an arrival rate of 0.8 orders a second (an order every 1.25 seconds, 48 a minute) gives exactly 1.2.

The formulas give no wait for two packers with gamma packing times, so the line under `Not estimated` says to measure it. [Queues and Capacity](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/#explain-the-load) works the same numbers out by hand.

`--verify` measures it. It runs the model unpaced and compares each statistic with the analysis, as [Check Against Theory](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/analysis/check-against-theory/index.md) shows. With `--replications`, it runs the model that many times from `--seed`, each to `--until`, and compares with each measure's 95% interval. `--target` sets the utilisation the hints aim for:

```bash
# Ten one-hour runs compared with the analysis, and hints for utilisation 0.9
desflow explain experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --verify --replications 10 --seed 42 --until 1h --target 0.9
```

```text
Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 0.4/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack (task, rate 0.4/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> exit
Resources
+---------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |    μ | c |   ρ | Wq | L | status |
|----------+-----+------+---+-----+----+---+--------|
| packers  | 0.4 | 0.25 | 2 | 0.8 |  - | - | OK     |
+---------------------------------------------------+
packers by units
+-----------------------+
| c |      ρ | status   |
|---+--------+----------|
| 1 |    1.6 | UNSTABLE |
| 2 |    0.8 | OK       |
| 3 | 0.5333 | OK       |
| 4 |    0.4 | OK       |
+-----------------------+
Bottleneck: packers
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times
Hints for utilisation 0.9:
  packers with 2 units: utilisation 0.8, at most 0.9
  packers with 2 units: utilisation 0.9 at a request every 2.22 seconds (27 a minute, 0.45 a second)
Verify: 10 runs to 3600 s, seed 42
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| node    | measure      | analysis | measured |        ± | result       |
|---------+--------------+----------+----------+----------+--------------|
| packers | utilization  |      0.8 |   0.7953 |  0.01561 | agrees       |
| packers | queue_length |        - |    1.823 |   0.2856 | not compared |
| pack    | wait         |        - |    4.505 |   0.6483 | not compared |
| orders  | throughput   |      0.4 |   0.4002 | 0.007201 | agrees       |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
Not compared:
  packers queue_length: no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times
  pack wait: no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times
--verify checks the implementation against the queueing analysis where it applies; it does not show that the model is close enough to the real system
```

The measured utilisation of 0.7953 and throughput of 0.4002 agree with the analysis, so the model does what the formulas say. The wait has no formula here, so the runs only measure it: 4.505 seconds. With a target of 0.9, the hints say that two packers reach it at an order every 2.22 seconds. `--json` prints the same explanation as one JSON object, for a script to read. Its `schema_version` names the shape, which the [`Explanation`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/api/#explaining-a-model) class describes:

```bash
desflow explain experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --json > explain.json
```

### Run It

`desflow run --sample` prints the first events as JSON lines. It runs the model unpaced, with no ingress, and with no sinks of the file's own, so a model that writes to Kafka or a database needs no service:

```bash
desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --sample 5
```

```text
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":3.1904748458705834,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","sim_id":"Shop","service":"packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":3.1904748458705834,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","sim_id":"Shop","service":"packing","status":"started"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":3.369806658930949,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-2","task":"pack","instance":1,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","sim_id":"Shop","service":"packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":3.369806658930949,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-2","task":"pack","instance":1,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","sim_id":"Shop","service":"packing","status":"started"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":4.671648089361866,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-3","task":"pack","instance":2,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","sim_id":"Shop","service":"packing","status":"queued"}}
```

Each order publishes `queued` when it joins the packers' queue and `started` when a packer takes it. The first two orders find a packer free, so each starts at the moment it queues. Without `--sample`, `desflow run` runs the model with its own settings and sinks. A model that runs out of events before the sample is full ends with exit 0 and the records it made.

`--var NAME=VALUE` fills `${NAME}` in the file and in the files it includes, before the environment does, and `check` and `test` take it too. `explain` and `experiment` do not take `--var`. `--watch` runs the file in a child process and runs it again whenever the file, or a `.py` file beside it, changes, so a change to a blueprint shows its first events at once. It needs the `watch` extra: `pip install "desflow[watch]"`. Press Ctrl+C to stop it:

```bash
desflow run shop.yaml --var PACKERS=3 --sample 5
desflow run shop.yaml --sample 5 --watch
```

One run is one sample, so measure the wait with [replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/index.md): the same model with ten seeds, each run for one hour:

```bash
desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --replications 10 --seed 42 --until 1h
```

```text
measure                                n          mean    half-width (95%)
resources.packers.capacity            10             2                   0
resources.packers.in_use              10           1.8              0.3016
resources.packers.queue_length        10             4               3.422
resources.packers.utilization         10            90               15.08
resources.packers.utilization_avg     10         79.53               1.561
resources.packers.queue_length_avg    10         1.823              0.2856
tasks.pack.in_progress                10           5.8               3.566
tasks.pack.finished                   10          1441               25.92
tasks.pack.wait_mean                  10         4.505              0.6483
tasks.pack.wait_max                   10         28.84               4.347
tasks.pack.service_mean               10         3.972             0.04102
tasks.pack.service_max                10         14.64              0.8328
flows.orders.finished                 10          1441               25.92
flows.orders.started                  10          1446               26.78
flows.orders.in_system                10           5.8               3.566

Seed 42; replication seeds: 2684470948, 4091952314, 233227757, 3276785861, 3644269654, 1206282609, 3543069911, 3479688010, 877132087, 1244265337
Repeat one replication with: desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --seed <its seed> --until 1h
```

The mean wait is 4.505 seconds, and its [half-width](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#interval-and-half-width) of 0.6483 says that the true mean lies within about 0.65 seconds of it, with 95% confidence. The packers are busy 79.53% of the time, close to the 0.8 that `explain` worked out. The last line repeats any one replication, with its events. This shop has no sinks. A model with a sink, such as `type: Console`, also sends the result to it as telemetry: one reading for each replication and measure. A Console sink therefore prints those lines before the table, as [What the Sinks Receive](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/#what-the-sinks-receive) explains.

`--measure` names a statistic to summarise, and repeats for more. `--level` sets the confidence level of the intervals. `--workers` runs that many replications at once, each in its own process, and gives the same results, because each replication keeps its seed:

```bash
# Two statistics at a 99% level, two replications at a time
desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --replications 10 --seed 42 --until 1h --measure tasks.pack.wait_mean --measure resources.packers.utilization_avg --level 0.99 --workers 2
```

```text
measure                               n          mean    half-width (99%)
tasks.pack.wait_mean                 10         4.505              0.9314
resources.packers.utilization_avg    10         79.53               2.243

Seed 42; replication seeds: 2684470948, 4091952314, 233227757, 3276785861, 3644269654, 1206282609, 3543069911, 3479688010, 877132087, 1244265337
Repeat one replication with: desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --seed <its seed> --until 1h
```

The means are the same as before. At 99%, the half-width of the mean wait grows from 0.6483 to 0.9314 seconds, because more confidence needs a wider interval.

`--stdout` prints the run's records as JSON lines, instead of writing to the file's sinks. The run keeps its ingress connectors, so a `KafkaIngress` still applies its `topic_policy`: it creates the control topic, and with `drop_and_create` it deletes it and creates it again. `--drain` stops the arrivals at the end time and runs on until every order has left. This run stops the arrivals at 20 seconds, and its last record is the ninth order packed, at 24.789303362278915 seconds. A record keeps its time unrounded:

```bash
# Every record of a 20-second run that drains, as JSON lines in a file
desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --seed 42 --until 20 --drain --stdout > records.jsonl
```

### Compare Designs

`desflow experiment` runs an [experiment](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiments/index.md): here two packers against three, 20 replications of each with the same seeds, with a check that three packers keep the mean wait under 2 seconds. `--output` names the folder for its files, here `results/packers` in the current folder. Without it, they go to the folder the file's `output` names, beside the file:

```bash
desflow experiment experiment/yaml/experiment.yaml --output results/packers
```

```text
Wrote the artifacts and report.md to results/packers
passed: three: tasks.pack.wait_mean max 2, checked 0.5919
```

The check passed: the upper end of the interval of the mean wait with three packers is 0.5919 seconds, under the bound of 2. The command exits with status 1 when a check fails, so a CI job that runs it fails too. The six files in `results/packers` hold every value, and `report.md` compares the designs, as [Experiment Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiment-results/index.md) describes. After editing `experiment.json` by hand, `desflow report` builds the report again from the files, without running anything:

```bash
desflow report results/packers
```

```text
Wrote results/packers/report.md
```

### Fit Measured Times

A packing time in a model comes from measured times. The `fitting` example holds 40 packing times measured at a bench, for a shop of its own, and `desflow fit` fits every family of times to them:

```bash
desflow examples get fitting --api yaml
desflow fit fitting/packing_times.csv --column packing_seconds --lower 0
```

```text
40 rows: 40 used, 0 missing, 0 invalid
family            status              AIC  KS stat KS p (approx.)  parameters or reason
exponential       rejected                                         its std is 1.5, the data's is 0.4832: more than 25% apart
normal            fitted            59.33    0.157         0.2504  mean=1.5, std=0.483218 (can draw below the lower bound 0)
lognormal         fitted            57.33  0.09406         0.8385  mean=1.50251, std=0.511854
truncated_normal  fitted            59.25   0.1558         0.2579  mean=1.49836, std=0.48579, low=0
constant          skipped                                          the values are not all equal
uniform           fitted            59.45    0.225        0.02923  low=0.7, high=2.7
triangular *      fitted            56.68   0.1258          0.511  low=0.546332, mode=1.2, high=2.83766
gamma             fitted            56.79   0.1157         0.6165  shape=9.55777, scale=0.15694
weibull           fitted            58.99   0.1502         0.2972  shape=3.33522, scale=1.67203
empirical         fitted                                           values: 40 numbers
* best: triangular
```

The first line counts the values. Each row is one family: `fitted` with its [AIC](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#aic-and-the-ks-test), where lower is better, or the reason it was not fitted. The `triangular` has the lowest AIC, 56.68, and the `gamma` is within 0.11 of it, so the data cannot tell the two apart. [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/#does-the-choice-matter) checks what the choice changes.

The other options shape the fit, as [Input Fitting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/input-fitting/index.md) describes:

- `--unit` names the data's unit, `ms`, `s`, `min` or `h`, and the settings are written in seconds.
- `--upper` is the highest plausible value, and a family that can draw above it is marked.
- `--candidates` names the families to try. The default is every family that fits times, ten of them. `poisson` and `geometric` count whole numbers, so a fit does not try them, and named in `--candidates` they are skipped with the reason that they count whole numbers.
- `--bins` offers the empirical distribution as a histogram with that many bins.
- `--min-count` is the fewest values a family is fitted to.
- `--tolerance` is how far a fitted mean and standard deviation may be from the data's, as a share of the data's. A tolerance that is negative or NaN, and a bound that is NaN, are refused, and so is a name in `--candidates` that is not a family, which the refusal quotes.
- `--drop-invalid` leaves out values that are not numbers or lie outside the bounds, instead of stopping.
- `--out` writes the best fit as YAML that a blueprint includes, and `--plot` draws the data against it as a PNG.

```bash
# Three families, a histogram of 8 bins, and the best fit written for the blueprint
desflow fit fitting/packing_times.csv --column packing_seconds --unit s --lower 0 --upper 10 --candidates triangular,gamma,empirical --bins 8 --min-count 30 --tolerance 0.2 --drop-invalid --out fitting/yaml/packing_fit.yaml --plot packing_fit.png
```

```text
40 rows: 40 used, 0 missing, 0 invalid
family            status              AIC  KS stat KS p (approx.)  parameters or reason
triangular *      fitted            56.68   0.1258          0.511  low=0.546332, mode=1.2, high=2.83766
gamma             fitted            56.79   0.1157         0.6165  shape=9.55777, scale=0.15694 (can draw above the upper bound 10)
empirical         fitted                                           edges: 9 numbers, counts: 8 numbers
* best: triangular
Wrote fitting/yaml/packing_fit.yaml
Wrote packing_fit.png
```

The `empirical` row is now a histogram of 8 bins, and the `gamma` row is marked because a gamma can draw above 10 seconds. `fitting/yaml/packing_fit.yaml` is the file the fitting example's blueprint includes, so `fitting/yaml/fitting.yaml` now draws its packing times from this triangular.

### Convert Parameters

A gamma takes a `shape` and a `scale`, not a mean and a standard deviation. `desflow dist` converts the measured times' mean of 1.5 seconds and standard deviation of 0.4832 seconds into them:

```bash
desflow dist gamma --mean 1.5 --std 0.4832
```

```text
parameters: shape 9.63671, scale 0.155655
mean 1.5, std 0.4832
variability: low (std / mean 0.322)
with no random generator, every draw is 1.5
YAML: {dist: gamma, shape: 9.63671, scale: 0.155655}
Python: dist="gamma", shape=9.63671, scale=0.155655
```

The shape and scale are close to the gamma that `desflow fit` found from the 40 values. The last two lines are the service in a blueprint and in the builder.

Given a family's own parameters, `desflow dist` converts the other way. Each of these lines prints the family's mean and standard deviation, as in the output above, for each kind of parameter: a rate, a constant's value, a low and a high, and a shape and a scale:

```bash
desflow dist exponential --rate 0.4
desflow dist constant --value 4
desflow dist uniform --low 0.7 --high 2.7
desflow dist gamma --shape 9.63671 --scale 0.155655
```

The shop's arrivals, `rate: 0.4`, are 2.5 seconds apart on average. A triangular also takes a mode, its most likely value. The one `desflow fit` found has a mean of 1.53 seconds, close to the measured 1.5:

```bash
desflow dist triangular --low 0.55 --mode 1.2 --high 2.84
```

```text
parameters: low 0.55, mode 1.2, high 2.84
mean 1.53, std 0.481785
variability: low (std / mean 0.315)
with no random generator, every draw is 1.53
YAML: {dist: triangular, low: 0.55, mode: 1.2, high: 2.84}
Python: dist="triangular", low=0.55, mode=1.2, high=2.84
```

`poisson` takes `--mean`, and `geometric` takes `--p`, the chance of success on each try. Both give whole numbers:

```bash
desflow dist geometric --p 0.25
```

`desflow dist` alone prints a table of every family with its parameters and a one-line summary, and [Choosing Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/choosing-inputs/#measured-times) explains the variability line:

```bash
desflow dist
```

### Set Up an Editor

`desflow schema` prints the JSON Schema of a blueprint, for the release you installed. An editor that reads it offers the keys as you type and marks a misspelt one:

```bash
desflow schema > blueprint.schema.json
```

[Set Up Your Editor](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/tools/set-up-your-editor/index.md) names the file in the editor's settings.

## How It Works

Each command reads its file and calls the library function a Python script would call. `desflow run` loads the model with `load_context` and runs it once, or calls `replicate` when `--replications` is given. `desflow experiment` calls `run_experiment`, `desflow report` calls `write_report`, and `desflow fit` reads the column and calls `fit_column`. `desflow dist`, `desflow schema` and `desflow examples` read the distribution table, the blueprint schema and the list of examples. A command therefore gives the same result as the Python call with the same arguments.

`desflow explain` takes the most steps. Look at them in order:

**Graph.** `explain` builds the graph from what the model declares: its arrivals, tasks, resources, stores, containers and `next` shares. It builds and runs nothing. Code the model does not declare, such as a hand-written arrival loop or an `add_process` function, becomes an opaque node. The graph also has an edge with no share from a task to each task it starts by an `on:` or `listen` spawn, a `task` branch of `wait`, `open` or `subscribe`, a spawn in the `on:` of a signal it fires, and `on_interrupt_next` and `on_interrupt_run`. `next` weights, fixed or computed, end no flow.

**Rates.** Each task's arrival rate comes from flow balance: the rate from its arrivals plus the share of each task that sends work to it. A `next` function or a hand-written arrival loop makes the rates unknown, because the graph cannot see where the work goes. A task reached by an edge with no share has no rate either, with the reason "how often starts it is not known before a run" or "the split after depends on the run".

**Coverage.** The formulas hold for a plain network of queues:

- Each task holds at most one resource.
- Each queue serves in arrival order, `fifo` or `lifo`, which give the same mean wait.
- Nothing blocks, removes, delays or reorders work by priority.

Anything else marks tasks, and the rate of a marked task is unknown. These mark tasks:

- A task feature, such as `put`, `patience`, `fail`, a `service_time` (`computed service time`) or an `interrupt` that names the task (`interruptions (an interrupt names it)`), marks that task and every task after it.
- An arrival feature gives the arrival no rate, so the tasks it starts have none: a `gap` (`computed gaps`), a `count`, `keys`, a `key` that can repeat or `max_events` (`limited or repeated arrivals`), a `group` other than 1, and `active: false`. A spawn `count` other than 1 is a feature too.
- A resource feature, such as `queue_limit`, breakdowns, a capacity that an `on:` entry sets, a resource family, or a resource picked by `key` or `lowest`, marks the tasks that use it and every task after them.
- A router with a weight that is an expression ends no flow and has no shares.
- A priority queue whose tasks have different priorities marks every task after its tasks. The resource keeps its utilisation but has no wait.
- An unstable resource marks every task after its tasks. The resource keeps its status.
- A scenario step, live ingress or an `add_process` function marks every arrival and every task.

A resource used by a marked task has no supported utilisation, status or wait, and the output names the reason under `Not estimated`.

**Waits.** The utilisation ρ is λ ÷ (c × μ): the arrival rate divided by the units times the rate one unit serves. The status follows from it. The wait depends on the units and the input:

- With no unit limit, the wait is 0.
- At one unit, the wait comes from Kingman's formula. It is exact when the input is Poisson, and an approximation when one arrival with other gaps feeds the resource's only task.
- At more than one unit, the wait comes from Erlang C, which needs Poisson arrivals and one exponential service time shared by every task that uses the resource.
- With any other input or times there is no wait, and the output says to run `--verify`.

Little's law then gives the queue length and the number in the system. The bottleneck is the resource with the highest supported utilisation. The hints solve the utilisation alone for the units and the arrival rate that reach `--target`.

**Verify.** `--verify` runs the model as one replication does: unpaced, with no ingress or egress, and with the `typical` statistics. It measures from the end of the warm-up to `--until`, or to the blueprint's `run.until` when `--until` is not given. It compares four measures with the analysis: each resource's utilisation and queue length, the wait of each task that holds one resource, and each arrival's throughput. A measure agrees with the analysis:

- For one run, when it is within 10% of the analysis, or measures 0 where the analysis gives 0.
- For replications, when it is within the 95% interval's half-width or 1%, whichever is larger.

A measure is not compared in these cases:

- The analysis has no value for it.
- Its resource is unstable.
- Its wait comes from Kingman's formula as an approximation.
- For a throughput, the arrival starts no task the graph shows, or its flow passes a marked task or an unstable resource.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

- **Inputs are files.** `run` reads a blueprint, or a builder file with `--sample` (not with `--stdout`, `--var` or `--watch`), `check` a blueprint or a builder file, `test` a blueprint or a builder file with a `tests.yaml`, `explain` a blueprint or a builder file with a module-level `SimulationContext`, `experiment` an experiment file, and `fit` a CSV file. For a Python model, use `replicate` and `run_experiment`, as [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/index.md) shows.
- **Examples need the network.** `examples get` downloads from GitHub at the installed release's tag. `--ref` picks another tag or branch.
- **`explain --json` is experimental.** Its shape can change in 1.x, and `schema_version` changes with it.
- **Exit statuses:** 0 on success, 1 on a failure, 2 on a usage error.
  - **1:** `run`, `check`, `test` or `explain` cannot load the file, a `test` differs from the measured statistics, an `experiment` check fails (its files are still written), `fit` finds no usable family, or `dist` has no formula from a mean and a standard deviation for the family.
  - **2:** a missing file, an option value that is not valid such as `--until abc`, a value that is not a number in a `fit` column, or an experiment file that is not valid.

# desflow run

The help of `desflow run`, generated from the command's code. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#run-it) uses this one on the shop, and its [What It Is](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#what-it-is) lists every command.

```text
Usage: desflow run [OPTIONS] {FILE}

  Build the simulation in FILE and run it, or run replications of it.

  FILE is a YAML blueprint. With --sample it may also be a builder file, a `.py`
  file with a module-level `SimulationContext`, which is imported as `desflow
  test` imports it, so its `if __name__ == "__main__":` block does not run.

Arguments:
  FILE  The blueprint file, or a builder file with --sample.  [required]

Options:
  --until TIME      Simulation time to stop at, in seconds or as a duration such
                    as '10 min'. Overrides run.until in the file.
  --seed N          The random seed. Overrides simulation.random_seed in the
                    file. A run without one logs the seed it drew, with the
                    command that repeats it.
  --drain           At the end time, stop the arrivals and keep running until
                    every entity in the model has left. Sets run.drain in the
                    file to true.
  --replications N  Run N replications unpaced, with seeds spawned from the
                    seed, and print the mean and confidence interval of each
                    statistic.  [x>=2]
  --level <float>   The confidence level of the replications' intervals, between
                    0 and 1.  [default: 0.95]
  --measure NAME    A statistic to summarise, such as tasks.pack.wait_mean;
                    repeat it for more. Defaults to every statistic the run
                    publishes, at least up to typical.
  --workers N       Replications run at once, each in its own process.
                    [default: 1; x>=1]
  --sample N        Print the first N events as JSON lines, unpaced, with no
                    ingress and no real sinks.  [x>=1]
  --stdout          Print every record except the system.simulation.lag_seconds
                    readings as a JSON line, instead of writing to the file's
                    sinks. The lag readings describe the wall clock, not the
                    model.
  --var NAME=VALUE  Fill ${NAME} in the file and in the files it includes,
                    before the environment does. Repeat it for more.
  --watch           Run in a child process, and run again whenever the file or a
                    .py file beside it changes. Needs the watch extra.
  --help            Show this message and exit.

  Examples:

    # Run a blueprint, sending its records to its sinks

    $ desflow run shop.yaml

    # Print the first five events, with no services

    $ desflow run shop.yaml --sample 5

    # Print every record as a JSON line instead of sending it

    $ desflow run shop.yaml --stdout

    # Run 20 replications and print the mean and interval of each
    statistic

    $ desflow run shop.yaml --replications 20 --seed 7

    # Print the first five events again whenever the file changes

    $ desflow run shop.yaml --sample 5 --watch
```

# desflow check

The help of `desflow check`, generated from the command's code. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#check-it-before-a-long-run) uses this one on the shop, and its [What It Is](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#what-it-is) lists every command.

```text
Usage: desflow check [OPTIONS] {FILE...}

  Check that each blueprint or builder file in FILE... builds, without running
  it.

  It reports what `desflow run` reports before the clock starts: YAML errors,
  unknown keys, missing names, unset variables, `!python` references that cannot
  be imported, and connectors whose extra is missing or whose settings are
  refused. A Parquet, Jsonl or Iceberg connector, in a blueprint or a builder
  file, is refused when its extra is not installed. It also reports a `tests`
  entry with no seed in a file with none, as `desflow test` does. It warns about
  a run with no end: an arrival with a `dist` or a `gap` and no `max_events`, in
  a file with no `run.until`, `run.stop` or `run.segments`. It does not call
  `run.before`, contact a broker, a database or a catalog, or run a `!python`
  function. Importing a `!python` module runs its top-level code, as `desflow
  run` does. A builder file, a `.py` file with a module-level
  `SimulationContext`, is imported as `desflow test` imports it, so an import
  whose extra is missing is reported; its `if __name__ == "__main__":` block
  does not run. An error or a `sys.exit` of the file's code is one line, with
  the file, its line and the error's type. Prints `ok FILE (sim_id ID)` for each
  valid file and every error of an invalid one, and exits 1 if any file is
  invalid.

Arguments:
  FILE...  The blueprint files, or builder files.  [required]

Options:
  --var NAME=VALUE  Fill ${NAME} in the files and in the files they include,
                    before the environment does. Repeat it for more.
  --help            Show this message and exit.

  Examples:

    # Check one blueprint without running it

    $ desflow check shop.yaml

    # Check every blueprint in a folder, as a pre-commit hook does

    $ desflow check examples/*.yaml

    # Check a builder file, which defines its model in Python

    $ desflow check shop.py
```

# desflow test

The help of `desflow test`, generated from the command's code. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#check-it-before-a-long-run) uses this one on the shop, and its [What It Is](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#what-it-is) lists every command.

```text
Usage: desflow test [OPTIONS] {FILE...}

  Run the tests of each file in FILE... and report the statistics that differ.

  A test names a seed, an end time and the statistics its run must give, such as
  tasks.pack_order.finished. It runs the model once, unpaced, with no ingress
  and no egress, so a test contacts no service. A test states its measures at
  one seed in one version of desflow: a new release may draw its random numbers
  differently, so exact seeded values are not promised across versions. Run it
  with --fix after an upgrade or a deliberate change and read the changes. A
  builder file reads its tests from a tests.yaml in its folder.

  Prints ok for each passing test, and each difference of a failing one. Exits 1
  if any test fails.

Arguments:
  FILE...  The blueprint files, or builder files with a tests.yaml beside them.
           [required]

Options:
  --fix             Write the statistics the runs gave into the expect values
                    that differ, and into a test with none, instead of reporting
                    differences. Read the changes before you keep them.
  --var NAME=VALUE  Fill ${NAME} in a blueprint and in the files it includes,
                    before the environment does. Repeat it for more.
  --help            Show this message and exit.

  Examples:

    # Check the tests in a blueprint

    $ desflow test shop.yaml

    # Write the statistics the runs gave into the expect values, then read
    them

    $ desflow test shop.yaml --fix
```

# desflow explain

The help of `desflow explain`, generated from the command's code. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#check-it-before-a-long-run) uses this one on the shop, and its [What It Is](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#what-it-is) lists every command.

```text
Usage: desflow explain [OPTIONS] {SOURCE}

  Show the model in SOURCE as a graph, with its utilisation, status, waits and
  tuning hints where the queueing formulas apply, and why where they do not.

Arguments:
  SOURCE  A YAML blueprint, or a builder Python file with a module-level
          SimulationContext, local or a URI such as s3://bucket/sims/shop.yaml.
          [required]

Options:
  --json            Print the explanation as JSON (schema_version 0,
                    experimental).
  --verify          Also run the model unpaced and compare its statistics with
                    the analysis.
  --until TIME      With --verify: the end of the run, in seconds or as a
                    duration such as '10 min'. Overrides run.until in the file.
  --seed N          With --verify: the run's seed. Overrides the model's own.
  --replications N  With --verify: run N times and compare with each measure's
                    95% interval, instead of one run within 10 percent.  [x>=2]
  --target T        The utilisation the hints aim for, above 0 and at most 10;
                    at 1 or above the hints are for deliberate overload.
                    [default: 0.85]
  --help            Show this message and exit.

  Examples:

    # Show the graph, the utilisation and the bottleneck

    $ desflow explain shop.yaml

    # Size each resource for a utilisation of 0.7

    $ desflow explain shop.yaml --target 0.7

    # Compare the formulas with 10 replications of the model

    $ desflow explain shop.yaml --verify --replications 10[/bold
    cyan]

    # Print the result as JSON

    $ desflow explain shop.yaml --json
```

# desflow fit

The help of `desflow fit`, generated from the command's code. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#fit-measured-times) uses this one on the shop, and its [What It Is](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#what-it-is) lists every command.

```text
Usage: desflow fit [OPTIONS] {FILE}

  Fit a column of FILE to the distribution families, and exit 1 if none is
  usable.

Arguments:
  FILE  A CSV file with a header row.  [required]

Options:
  --column NAME                   The column to fit.  [required]
  --unit <str>                    The data's unit: ms, s, min or h. Settings are
                                  in seconds.  [default: s]
  --candidates NAMES              The families to try, separated by commas.
                                  Defaults to every family.
  --lower <float>                 The lowest plausible value, in the data's
                                  unit.
  --upper <float>                 The highest plausible value, in the data's
                                  unit.
  --bins <int range>              Offer the empirical distribution as a
                                  histogram with this many bins.  [x>=1]
  --min-count <int range>         The fewest values a family is fitted to.
                                  [default: 20; x>=1]
  --tolerance <float>             How far a fitted mean and standard deviation
                                  may be from the data's, as a share of the
                                  data's.  [default: 0.25]
  --drop-invalid / --no-drop-invalid
                                  Leave out invalid values rather than stopping.
                                  [default: no-drop-invalid]
  --out FILE                      Write the best candidate's settings here, for
                                  !include in a blueprint.
  --plot FILE                     Draw the data against the best candidate, as a
                                  PNG.
  --help                          Show this message and exit.

  Examples:

    # Fit measured packing times, in seconds

    $ desflow fit times.csv --column packing_seconds

    # Write the best fit's settings for a blueprint to load

    $ desflow fit times.csv --column packing_seconds --lower 0 --out
    packing.yaml
```

# desflow dist

The help of `desflow dist`, generated from the command's code. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#convert-parameters) uses this one on the shop, and its [What It Is](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#what-it-is) lists every command.

```text
Usage: desflow dist [OPTIONS] [FAMILY]

  List the distribution families, or convert parameters to a mean and std and
  back.

  Exits 1 for a family with no formula from a mean and std.

Arguments:

Options:

  --mean X   The mean, a parameter or, with --std, the mean to convert from.
  --std X    The std, a parameter or, with --mean, the std to convert from.
  --low X    The lowest value.
  --value X  A constant's time.
  --high X   The highest value.
  --mode X   The most likely value.
  --shape X  The shape.
  --scale X  The scale.
  --p X      The chance of success on each try.
  --help     Show this message and exit.

  Examples:
```

# Agent Skill

# Agent Skill

The desflow skill gives an AI coding assistant the rules of the library, so that it writes, checks, tests and runs desflow models instead of guessing them.

It is one of the ways desflow makes a simulation quicker to build. A [YAML blueprint](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/blueprints/index.md) describes a whole model with no Python. The skill lets an assistant write that blueprint for you and check it. [From history to simulation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/about/roadmap/#from-history-to-simulation), planned after 1.0, starts a model from an event log.

The skill is a folder, `skills/desflow/`, in the Agent Skills format that Claude Code and other assistants read. An assistant that supports the format loads the skill when a request mentions desflow, a blueprint, a test of a simulation model, or a SimPy model that streams records. The folder is generated from the code, so it lists what the release has.

______________________________________________________________________

## Tasks

Each page gives the request to type, what the skill tells the assistant to do, and the result on one example: the shop of the [Learn tutorial](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md), one packer and an order every 2 seconds, drafted from a description in words.

| Task                                                                                        | What the assistant gives you                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Draft a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/draft-a-model/index.md)               | a blueprint from a description of a process, with each assumed number marked, checked against queueing theory |
| [Port a SimPy Program](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/port-a-simpy-program/index.md) | a desflow model that does what a SimPy program does, compared with the program's output                       |
| [Write Another Form](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/write-another-form/index.md)     | the Builder and Low-level forms of a blueprint, which give the same records                                   |
| [Write Tests](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/write-tests/index.md)                   | tests of the statistics with `desflow test`, with expected values taken from the request                      |
| [Run a Study](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/run-a-study/index.md)                   | replications with a confidence interval, and a comparison of designs with `desflow experiment`                |
| [Fit a Distribution](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/fit-a-distribution/index.md)     | a distribution fitted to measured times with `desflow fit`, loaded into the model                             |

______________________________________________________________________

## Install the Skill

1. Install desflow, so the assistant can run the `desflow` commands that [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/index.md) shows, such as `desflow explain` and `desflow run`.

1. Copy `skills/desflow/` into the skills folder of the assistant. Take it from the repository at the tag of the release you installed: `v` followed by what `desflow --version` prints. For Claude Code, `~/.claude/skills/desflow/` is for every project and `.claude/skills/desflow/` in a project is for that project. With git, these lines copy it for every project:

   ```bash
   # The source of the installed release, which holds the skill
   git clone --depth 1 --branch "v$(desflow --version)" https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow /tmp/desflow-src
   mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
   cp -R /tmp/desflow-src/skills/desflow ~/.claude/skills/desflow
   ```

   The block is for a first install. Before you run it again, delete `/tmp/desflow-src` and `~/.claude/skills/desflow`, because `git clone` stops at an existing folder and `cp -R` would put the new copy inside the old one. If `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is set, use that folder in place of `~/.claude`, here and in the check below.

1. Ask the assistant for a model, such as "write a desflow blueprint for a shop with two packers and a lunch rush, and run it". It reads the skill when the request mentions desflow or a blueprint.

With the GitHub CLI, one command does the copy. `gh skill install` is a preview command of the GitHub CLI, so it needs `gh` 2.90.0 or later:

```bash
gh skill install jaehyeon-kim/desflow desflow --agent claude-code --scope user
```

`--scope user` installs for every project, in your home folder. `--scope project`, the default, installs for the current project, inside its git repository, so run it from that repository. Another assistant takes its own `--agent` value, listed in `gh skill install --help`. Without `--agent`, `gh` asks which assistant to install for. When it cannot ask, it installs for GitHub Copilot. At project scope, Copilot uses `.agents/skills`, a folder several other assistants also read. `gh` installs the latest release. `desflow@v<version>` in place of `desflow` pins one, with `<version>` the release you installed.

______________________________________________________________________

## Check the Install

The folder must hold `SKILL.md`, and Claude Code lists the skills it has loaded with `/skills`, where `desflow` must appear:

```bash
ls ~/.claude/skills/desflow/SKILL.md
```

______________________________________________________________________

## Other Ways to Teach an Assistant

- **Schema.** Give the assistant `https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/schema/blueprint.schema.json`, or the output of `desflow schema`, to validate what it writes.
- **Documentation as text.** `https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/llms.txt` is an index of the pages, and `https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/llms-full.txt` holds all of them in one file.

______________________________________________________________________

## Sources

The folder layout and the `SKILL.md` fields follow the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification). The folders Claude Code reads are in its [skills documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills). The `gh skill install` flags are those of `gh skill install --help` in GitHub CLI 2.95.0.

# Draft a Model

Describe a process in your own words, and an assistant with the skill turns it into a blueprint. It marks every number it had to assume, checks the load against queueing theory, and runs a study before it gives you an answer.

The GIF follows one request, the packing shop of the [Learn tutorial](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md), through the steps the skill teaches:

The sections below hold each step's text, so you can copy the request and check each answer.

______________________________________________________________________

## Ask

Paste the request into an assistant that has the skill:

```text
A shop packs customer orders.
An order arrives about every 2 seconds.
One packer packs each order in about 1.5 seconds.
How long does an order wait?
```

______________________________________________________________________

## Draft

The skill tells the assistant to start from the nearest example (`desflow examples list`), and to build the model in stages, running the file after each one. It asks you for the numbers the description does not give. When it has to assume one, it marks it with a comment and lists the assumed numbers first in its reply, because you must confirm them.

The description does not say whether orders arrive at random or how much the packing time varies. The draft assumes both:

```yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0  # no pacing: the run ends as soon as it is done
  random_seed: 42
  # a fixed date, so two runs give the same records
  logical_start_time: '2026-01-05T09:00:00Z'

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}  # said: one packer

services:
  # said: 1.5 seconds; assumed: every order takes the same time
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # said: an order every 2 seconds on average; assumed: orders arrive at random
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
```

The skill drafts a blueprint, so the drafted model is the YAML tab. [Write Another Form](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/write-another-form/index.md) has its Builder form.

The skill drafts a blueprint, so the drafted model is the YAML tab. [Write Another Form](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/write-another-form/index.md) has its Low-level form.

______________________________________________________________________

## Check the Load

Before it runs anything, the assistant checks that the packer can keep up. `desflow explain` gives the queueing formulas' answer:

```bash
desflow explain drafted_shop.yaml
```

```text
Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 0.5/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack_order (task, rate 0.5/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> exit
Resources
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |      μ | c |    ρ |   Wq |     L | status |
|----------+-----+--------+---+------+------+-------+--------|
| packers  | 0.5 | 0.6667 | 1 | 0.75 | 2.25 | 1.875 | OK     |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
Bottleneck: packers
Hints for utilisation 0.85:
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 0.75, at most 0.85
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 0.85 at a request every 1.76 seconds (34 a minute, 0.5667 a second)
```

The packer is busy 75% of the time (`ρ`), so the queue does not grow without limit, and the formulas give a mean wait of 2.25 seconds (`Wq`). When a model routes on a variable or has scenario steps, `desflow explain` gives no estimate, and the skill tells the assistant to check the load by hand: the work of one case, times the arrival rate, must fit inside the capacity. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#check-it-before-a-long-run) shows more of `desflow explain`, and [Run a Study](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/run-a-study/index.md) compares designs.

______________________________________________________________________

## Answer From Replications

One run is one sample, so the skill tells the assistant to answer from replications. 20 runs of an hour, each with its own seed spawned from 42:

```bash
desflow run drafted_shop.yaml --replications 20 | grep -E "^measure|wait_mean"
```

```text
measure                                n          mean    half-width (95%)
tasks.pack_order.wait_mean            20         2.383              0.1828
```

The mean wait is 2.38 ± 0.18 seconds. The interval, 2.20 to 2.57, holds the 2.25 of the formulas, so the model and the theory agree. The run starts with an empty shop and has no warm-up, which [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) explains how to choose.

______________________________________________________________________

## Check the Reply

The skill tells the assistant to copy a checklist into its reply and tick each line: every behaviour the request names, the key that makes it, the record that shows it, and a run of the skill's own check on the files. Read the assumed numbers first. Then check that the answer is an interval from replications, not the result of one run.

______________________________________________________________________

# Port a SimPy Program

Ask for a port when you have a SimPy program and want its records streamed, its parameters changed during a run, or its study run with desflow's tools. An assistant with the skill writes a desflow model that does what the program does, and compares the two outputs.

______________________________________________________________________

## Ask

```text
Port shop.py, a SimPy program, to desflow.
Keep its behaviour, and compare its mean wait with the desflow model's.
```

______________________________________________________________________

## What the Assistant Does

The skill gives the assistant a table of the places where desflow behaves differently from SimPy, each with what to write in the port. It checks each row against the program before it writes the model. Some of the rows:

- A program that counts time in minutes has each time converted to its unit, such as `mean: 4 min`, because a bare number is seconds.
- A signal fires once by default. One that the program fires more than once gets `once: false`.
- A `put` with no `yield` in the program becomes a `put` with `wait: false`, which goes on at once.
- A failure no task handles stops the run. A program that goes on after a child process fails gets `on_unhandled_failure: continue`.

It picks the way to write the model as for any model: YAML when the program is resources, arrivals and tasks, and the Low-level API when it needs SimPy itself. Then it runs both and compares them: the records with `desflow run <file> --sample`, or the statistics over replications, within their intervals.

______________________________________________________________________

## Example

[Coming from SimPy](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/coming-from-simpy/index.md) ports the shop, written as a plain SimPy program in the four classes most tutorials teach. Both versions run 10 times for an hour, and their mean waits agree within their intervals. [SimPy Examples](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/examples/index.md) ports the seven examples that ship with SimPy, each in YAML, the Builder and the Low-level API, and compares each with the program's output.

______________________________________________________________________

## Check the Reply

Check that the reply names each row of the table that applies to the program, and what the port writes for it. Then check the comparison: the same records at the same times, or statistics whose intervals overlap. [SimPy Compatibility](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/compatibility/index.md) lists every SimPy feature with its form in desflow.

# Write Another Form

Ask for the Builder or Low-level form of a blueprint when the model needs Python, such as a payload function, or SimPy itself. An assistant with the skill writes a form that gives the same records as the blueprint, and checks that it does.

______________________________________________________________________

## Ask

```text
Write the Builder and Low-level forms of drafted_shop.yaml.
They must give the same records as the YAML at the same seed.
```

______________________________________________________________________

## What the Assistant Does

The skill gives the assistant the rules that keep the forms equal:

- A time in YAML and in the Builder takes a unit. The Low-level `DistributionConfig` takes seconds only, so the unit goes in a comment.
- The Low-level form draws each time through `sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config("<sim_id>.<path>"))`, as the YAML does, so it draws the same numbers at the same seed.
- Builder and Low-level code use only the names `from desflow import ...` gives, never a private attribute.
- A Python file runs with `python <file>` and prints its records with `ConsoleEgress(format="json")`.

Then it runs the skill's check on the three files. The check runs each form at the model's seed and the two after it, and compares every record with the YAML's:

```bash
python <skill folder>/scripts/check_model.py drafted_shop.yaml drafted_shop_builder.py drafted_shop_low_level.py
```

```text
ok desflow check
ok imports
ok runs of the Python files
ok seed and start time
ok records of the forms
ok desflow test
```

Each line is a check that passed. A failed check names the file and line, and what to write instead. `seed and start time` fails on a model without a fixed `logical_start_time`, because the timestamps of two runs then differ, so the drafted shop sets one.

______________________________________________________________________

## Full Files

The three forms of the shop from [Draft a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/ai/draft-a-model/index.md). [Writing a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/index.md) explains how the three ways relate.

Full files

```yaml
  # packer's time. Over 10 hours it varies by about 0.5 between seeds, so 2 is four
```
